question: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because she is concerned he is having another stroke. The patient says he woke up with right-sided facial weakness and drooping. Past medical history is significant for a recent case of shingles treated with acyclovir, and a stroke, diagnosed 10 years ago, from which he recovered with no residual functional deficits. On physical examination, there is weakness and drooping of the entire right side of the face. Sensation is intact. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following additional findings would also most likely be seen in this patient?

options.opc: Complete loss of taste to the tongue

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Right-sided facial weakness and drooping" -> "involvement of facial nerve" -> "decreased function of facial muscles" -> "decreased salivation due to involvement of parasympathetic fibers in facial nerve" -> 75%

CHAIN: "Right-sided facial weakness and drooping" -> "involvement of facial nerve" -> "facial nerve also innervates stapedius muscle in the ear" -> "partial hearing loss due to dysfunction of stapedius muscle" -> 70%

CHAIN: "Right-sided facial weakness and drooping" -> "involvement of facial nerve" -> "facial nerve affects taste sensation in anterior two-thirds of the tongue" -> "complete loss of taste to the tongue" -> 60%

CHAIN: "Right-sided facial weakness and drooping" -> "involvement of facial nerve" -> "facial nerve does not affect forehead muscles in upper motor neuron lesions" -> "wrinkled forehead due to preserved innervation by bilateral upper motor neurons" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Right-sided facial weakness and drooping" -> "involvement of facial nerve" -> "facial nerve does not affect language processing areas" -> "expressive aphasia unlikely unless additional brain areas are affected" -> 20%
analysis: The patient presents with weakness and drooping of the entire right side of the face, with intact sensation. This clinical presentation is consistent with Bell's palsy, a peripheral facial nerve palsy. In Bell's palsy, the forehead is also affected due to the involvement of the lower motor neuron, unlike central facial palsies where the forehead is spared due to bilateral upper motor neuron input. Therefore, the inability to wrinkle the forehead would be a likely finding in this case.
